cards.title: Founder ads present an argument, not a founder monologue
cards.summary: Reframe founder ad production as scripting the founder's argument around the viewer's problem rather than filming a founder talking about themselves.
cards.use_when: Planning a founder-led video shoot or briefing a script for paid social acquisition creative.
steps: Treat the ad as the founder's argument, not a raw iPhone video of the founder: the format works because it carries authenticity, authority and trust from a real person, not because the founder is interesting.
Do not stop at 'put the founder on camera': authenticity alone underperforms. The ad needs a scripted structure that delivers the argument.
Write through the viewer's eyes: lead with an underlying desire or problem the audience already has, then use the founder story as the lens, not the subject.

Show the viewer themselves in the story ('this happened to me too') and problem-agitate so they keep watching, open a curiosity gap around a solution, walk them through the mechanism, then close the loop.
Before recording, confirm the script would still make sense if a non-founder delivered it — if yes, the founder may be optional and the script is doing the work.
caveats: The source asserts nobody cares about the founder's story by itself; some founder-story-only ads do work, but the majority underperform.
Do not invent a founder story you cannot stand behind — the source calls fabricated founder stories black hat and a risk to future exit value.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Highest-performing founder ad script structure: claim, proof, mechanism, CTA
cards.summary: Use the Claim → Proof of Claim → Unique Mechanism (founder story) → Proof of Mechanism → CTA/Social Proof sequence identified from top-spending founder ads.
cards.use_when: Drafting the body script for a founder video ad for cold acquisition traffic.
steps: Open with an adversarial claim that doubles as a hook, e.g. 'the industry is lying about X' or 'big supermarkets sell you Y that is full of plastic'.
Immediately prove the claim — the source found no top performer that made a claim without proof. Example framing: 'a study found competitors contain 1/100 of the stated ingredient'.
Move into the unique mechanism tied to the founder story: the adversarial problem existed, competitors did the bad thing, so the founder built the differentiated solution.
Layer more proof onto the mechanism (factory visits, third-party testing, ingredient labels, certificates) so the viewer believes the mechanism is real.
Close with the CTA — how to buy, the offer, scarcity and urgency — plus customer social proof.
Keep the CTA simple: average watch time means few viewers reach it, so the source does not bother testing multiple CTAs on the same body.
caveats: This structure was the top performer among the source's own top-spending founder ads in their ad account; it is a source-specific finding, not a universal ranking.
Adversarial competitor claims carry compliance and legal risk — the source notes founders are often more willing than agencies to take that risk.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Batch-shoot founder ads: pairing hooks with bodies
cards.summary: Multiply one shoot into dozens of ads by combining multiple hooks with a few distinct body scripts rather than shooting ads one by one.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a founder shoot and deciding how much creative volume to generate from one session.
steps: Prep distinct body scripts that tell materially different stories — not minor rewordings.
Build a hook set for each body, then cross-combine: e.g. 10 hooks × 3 bodies = 30 ads.
Optionally add a second CTA/social-proof ending to reach higher counts, but the source does not recommend testing CTAs since so few viewers reach them.
Keep each hook contextually bridged into the body so the transition makes sense — mismatched hooks are a common failure in founder talking-head ads.
Expect the actual recording time to be small (about 4–5 minutes of camera time for this volume) and put the effort into scripting and production, not filming.
Scale volume by system, not headcount: the source reports clients producing 200–400 ads a month with one or two people on the content team.
caveats: Large agency-scale volumes cited (hundreds of ads per month, 1–2 person teams) are the source's client examples, not a benchmark every store should attempt.
Hooks that do not connect to the body break the ad even if they tested well in isolation.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Founder face is a sameness signal: diversify concept and format
cards.summary: Repeated talking-head founder ads fatigue because the founder's face creates sameness; fix with true concept diversification plus format and scene variation.
cards.use_when: A founder ad has started to fatigue and you are deciding what to shoot next.
steps: Diagnose whether the problem is format fatigue or concept fatigue: the same face, scene and talking-head delivery serving the same audience decays quickly.

Attack format first because it is easy: reshoot the identical script in a new location. The source reports taking a fatigued in-gym ad and running another $40,000 of spend through it by only changing the scene.
Stretch into new formats as volume grows: tier-list videos, founder walking a store aisle interacting with competitor products, or other organic-style formats instead of another talking head.
Attack concept next by changing one of three levers: the persona being addressed, the angle/unique mechanism, or the offer.

Note the source's difficulty ordering: offering a new or different product is easiest, changing the angle is hard because there may be only one true mechanism, and changing persona is hardest for founder ads because the founder must credibly represent that persona.
caveats: The $40,000 incremental spend figure is one source example, not a repeatable benchmark.
Reusing the same script is acceptable when editing or scenes vary substantially; the source frames this as true under current Meta conditions.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Use portfolio theory: never let founder ads carry the whole account
cards.summary: High-performing founder ads can generate enormous revenue but also decay; keep other formats alive instead of overweighting one concept.
cards.use_when: Deciding budget allocation across creative formats after a founder ad becomes a top spender.
steps: Treat total creative production like a portfolio: no single ad or concept should become the whole business.

Watch for the failure pattern the source describes — brands riding one founder ad with a few hook swaps to $20–30M, then hitting full audience saturation and decaying because they only produce founder ads.
Keep VSLs, statics and animation/claymation formats running alongside founder ads so sales do not depend on one fatigued concept.
Lean into a winner by making more variants, but maintain parallel output in other formats.
Recognize founder ads as one of the highest-spend single-ad categories the source has seen, alongside VSLs — high reward with concentration risk.
caveats: The $20–30M single-ad revenue figures are the source's own exposure to brands that collapsed after the ad fatigued, not an expected outcome.
Founder ads are described as optional for large brands — not the bottleneck for many eight- to nine-figure businesses — but they can improve performance when executed well.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Founder involvement spectrum: protagonist, voice, evidence, proxy, absent
cards.summary: Choose how much of the founder appears in each ad — face, voice only, evidence, proxy, or fully absent — to create format diversity from the same script.
cards.use_when: A founder is camera-shy, time-constrained, or you need format diversification without new concepts for paid social.
steps: Top of the spectrum: on-camera talking-head founder, which is ideal but the most fatigue-prone.
Voice-only: founder narrates over B-roll, animation or UGC footage — useful when the founder is uncomfortable on camera.
Evidence: no speaking, but use founder photos in a lab, certificates, or a shot of them walking through the factory facing away from camera.
Proxy: an employee, dietitian or supplier tells the founder story — less effective than the founder, but workable when the founder wants no face, voice or evidence involvement.
Absent: animation/AI formats which can visually demonstrate the problem and mechanism (e.g. showing cells changing) while telling the same founder story end to end.
Run the same script and concept across multiple levels of the spectrum to generate format diversification quickly.
caveats: Effectiveness generally decreases as you move away from the founder actually telling the story.
As you move toward proxy and absent, the format stretches away from being a true founder ad.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Change the founder's role in the script to multiply concepts
cards.summary: Move the founder between protagonist, witness, interviewer and reader roles to generate materially different scripts from the same story.
cards.use_when: You need new founder ad concepts without new founder stories, especially on smaller teams that cannot pay creators.
steps: Protagonist (most founder ads): first-person 'I built this because…'.
Witness: first person but observed — 'a customer emailed me last week and said…'.
Interviewer: the founder asks someone else (lab, manufacturing, design team) why they do something that benefits the customer.
Reader: the founder reads a review aloud — e.g. a one-star review — scripted so it still walks through the buyer's stages of awareness.
Mix this with other levers (persona, offer, proof type, stage of awareness) to reach roughly 20–30 distinct concepts from a small base.
caveats: The source says role-switching is high leverage for six- and seven-figure businesses that want volume without paying creators, but less necessary on eight- to ten-figure brands where founder time is scarce and these ads can run on non-founders.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Founder ad concept matrix: persona × awareness × angle × offer × proof × role
cards.summary: Generate founder ad concepts systematically by varying six variables to address different buyer types with matching proof.
cards.use_when: Building a new batch of founder ad concepts and deciding who each ad targets and what offer it carries.
steps: Variable 1 — persona/stage of awareness: e.g. skeptical first-time category buyer at problem awareness; existing category buyer at solution awareness; gift buyer at product awareness.
Variable 2 — angle: for first-time buyers, 'the entire category is lying to you'; for existing buyers in dosed CPG, an incorrect-dosage angle; for gift buyers, a taste angle.

Variable 3 — offer: single SKU for the first-time buyer; for the dosage angle, a bundle justified in the script because the second product makes the primary one work; a gifting pack for the gift buyer.
Variable 4 — proof type matched to the angle: lab certificate for the first-time buyer, competitor teardown for the dosage angle, an email read for the taste/gift angle.
Variable 5 — founder role: protagonist, witness, interviewer or reader.
Then mix and match any single variable to create a new concept — swapping role alone gives four versions of each base ad.
caveats: Stage-of-awareness changes also shift which proof and angle are appropriate, so do not change the persona label without adjusting the supporting proof.
The specific examples (creatine, makeup, beef jerky) are illustrative; apply the variable logic to your own category.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Static vs renewable founder story elements
cards.summary: Separate founder story components that must stay consistent from those you can refresh weekly to keep producing new ads.
cards.use_when: Planning ongoing founder ad production and deciding what to source and script each month.
steps: Keep static (changing them costs credibility): the origin story, why the company started, and the founder's personal problem.
Add value if you can: co-founder stories, including why the two founders' problems met in the middle — this multiplies available origin material.

Treat as renewable: customer reviews and emails (they change weekly), the support inbox, supplier calls and interviews (relevant as products and suppliers evolve), one-star reviews, and ongoing day-to-day conversations or in-person complaints.
Mine one-star reviews deliberately as script material — the source treats them as a constant for brands with meaningful volume and a format the founder can read on camera.
Refresh ads by swapping only the renewable variables while holding the origin story consistent.
caveats: Founder story material is finite: there is one true origin story with many ways to tell it, not an infinite supply of new stories.
Fabricating or changing origin facts is called black hat by the source and a risk to exit value.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Run founder ad production as a collection pipeline
cards.summary: Treat founder content as a monthly production system: hoard raw customer and supplier material continuously, then script and shoot in concentrated blocks.
cards.use_when: Setting up an ongoing founder ad cadence with limited founder time.
steps: Decide a monthly output target for founder ads as part of the broader creative mix (the source's illustration is 40 per month).
Build collection systems: pipe reviews into a database, route the support inbox into an AI model you can pull weekly for ad-relevant language, and record or note supplier calls and comms.
Capture one-star reviews, ongoing conversations and in-person complaints, and ask of each: could this become content?
Store everything so scripting sessions start from collected raw material instead of a blank page.
Shoot in concentrated blocks — once a month for general content, perhaps once a quarter with the founder — because the founder need not be on camera daily.
The source reports shooting enough founder ads in a one- to two-hour block to cover three to four months.
caveats: The 40-ads-a-month and one-to-two-hour shoot figures are source illustrations, not universal targets.
This pipeline assumes someone owns collection and scripting; without that, concentrated shoots produce generic content.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Founder video production quality rules
cards.summary: Founder ads must be edited like real ads — dynamic cuts, overlays, relevant hooks, natural delivery and varied scenes — not raw talking head uploads.
cards.use_when: Preparing a founder shoot and post-production for paid social creative.
steps: Do not upload an unedited talking head: use fast dynamic editing, overlays and engagement techniques that would retain viewers on organic content.
If shooting a talking-head founder story, use two cameras and incorporate motion.
Make every hook contextually relevant to the body — a hook about something that happened 10 years ago must connect to what the body actually discusses.
If the founder struggles with a teleprompter, script only the sentence-by-sentence structure and let them speak off script so delivery feels natural.
Change scenery as much as possible within the shoot window — even moving around one location adds immediate format diversification for the same script.
Expect new founders to be robotic for roughly the first 10 hours on camera; the source treats this as a normal ramp, not evidence that founder ads do not work.
caveats: The '10 hours' figure is the source's informal observation, not measured data.
Founder ads shot without these production standards are a common reason brands wrongly conclude the format does not work.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Hook variation: 2–4 per body, up to 8, never 30
cards.summary: Keep hook variations per founder body in the 2–4 range (up to about 8) so testing budget is not spread too thin.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many hook variants to launch per founder ad body in a paid social test.
steps: Set the natural limit first: only so many hooks can bridge naturally and contextually into a given body.
Aim for 2–4 hooks per body as the working range; the source accepts up to about 8.
Do not split a modest daily budget across 20–40 hook variants just to hit volume — the source warns that thin distribution prevents the ad set from exiting learning and gathering conversions.
Balance example from the source: spreading $1,000/day across three ads tests better than spreading the same budget across 20–40.
Reshoot hooks on existing winners, especially in new locations, to squeeze more spend from a fatigued high performer.
Remember most viewers never pass the hook, so hook optimization is high leverage — a loser can become a winner with a hook swap.
caveats: The source has run bodies with 40 hook variations and bodies with 9, so this is a practical sweet spot, not an absolute cap.
The $1,000/day figure is an illustrative budget split, not a recommended minimum spend.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Run founder ads through the founder's handle as partnership ads
cards.summary: Running founder ads via the founder's account rather than the company page usually performs better, with the lift tied to the founder's existing relevant content.
cards.use_when: Choosing placement and ad account identity for founder video ads.
steps: Compare the same founder creative run through the company page versus a partnership ad through the founder's handle.
Expect directionally better results from the founder's handle, but modest: the source cites roughly 5%–30% better performance, primarily driven by the founder's credibility and existing content.

Check whether the founder's personal profile has relevant content posting regularly. The source's own ads sit at the high end of that range because the founder's page has high organic volume and frequent posting.
If the founder's page has no relevant content (photos of daily life do not count), the lift is likely small and keeping ads on the company page avoids making the brand dependent on the individual.
Weigh the trade-off: company-page ads build brand association; partnership ads mean customers may buy from the founder rather than the brand.
caveats: The 5%–30% range is the source's firsthand experience, not a guaranteed uplift.
The decision is described as nuanced and case-dependent, not always-run-through-the-founder's-handle.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Founder ads are optional, and your exit terms may care
cards.summary: Founder ads can improve performance at any size, but they are a content type rather than a necessity, and heavy dependence on the founder's face can complicate an exit.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in founder-led creative or in other channels and formats.
steps: Do not treat founder ads as mandatory: the source says a $200M brand does not need the founder on camera to reach $300M, because creative format is unlikely to be the bottleneck at that scale.
Consider founder ads anyway for general performance lift when executed well.
Factor in cost structure: founder time is the primary production cost, which is favorable for small brands that would otherwise pay agencies, freelancers or creators.

Use the founder story to differentiate commoditized products (fashion, commodity supplements) by repositioning around a specific persona and problem rather than competing on the mechanism everyone else sells.

Flag exit risk: if founder ads hold a large share of spend, buyers may mark founder dependence in the term sheet — the source raises this as a real consideration, not a reason to avoid founder content.
caveats: The source's claim that founder ads perform better when good is explicitly a generalization, not a universal rule.
The exit/term-sheet concern is the source's characterization and varies by buyer and deal.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Differentiate a commodity product through the founder's story
cards.summary: When the product category is saturated and undifferentiated, reposition via the founder's specific problem and mechanism instead of competing on the product itself.
cards.use_when: Developing ad angles for a commoditized product where every competitor advertises the same mechanism.
steps: Identify the saturated mechanism everyone sells (e.g. electrolytes, creatine), and avoid competing there directly.

Build a specific persona-problem-story chain: who the founder was (e.g. a marathon runner), the specific problem they hit (dehydration), why existing solutions failed (XYZ), and therefore what they built.
Aim the story at a narrow persona with a specific problem rather than the whole category.
Use the founder's origin, mechanism and adversarial angle as the elements only the founder (or a credentialed expert) can credibly deliver.

Layer customer experience and diverse persona callouts separately — the source argues the founder's own product praise is lower credibility because the founder is biased; customers who match the viewer's problem carry it better.
caveats: This is the source's argument for why founder ads work, illustrated with hypothetical examples; it does not report controlled results.
Calling the founder's story a 'mechanism' is the source's terminology — it acknowledges the story is differentiation, not a true unique mechanism.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx
